deep.reconstruction:
Context. Folio 16r belongs to Riemann's ether notes. The previous page (40) set up a Gauss 'least constraint' (Zwang) functional for ether displacement u, ponderable bodies y and electricity z. This page continues in three threads.

(A) Gauss's principle of least constraint for a continuum (top left).
Header: the wave operator d²u/dt² − α²Σ_ι d²u/dx_ι², applied to each component, with the incompressibility constraint div u = ∂u1/∂x1 + ∂u2/∂x2 + ∂u3/∂x3 = 0.
The constraint functional is
Z = ∫ [ ½ Σ (∂²u/∂t²)² − α² Σ_ι (∂²u/∂x_ι²)(∂²u/∂t²) ] dx.
Integrating by parts (boundary terms dropped; this step is mine) turns this into
Z = ∫ [ ½ |ü|² + α² Σ_ι (∂u/∂x_ι)(∂³u/∂x_ι∂t²) ] dx.

Riemann then justifies Z from Gauss's principle with potential
X = ½ ∫ α² Σ_ι (∂u/∂x_ι)² dx.
He writes the requirement as
δ[ ∫ Σ (d ∂u/∂t)² + X(t+dt) ] = 0,
expanding X(t+dt) = X + (∂X/∂t) dt + (∂²X/∂t²) dt²/2 and using d(∂u/∂t) = ü dt.
- Only ü is varied.
- The ü-dependent part of ∂²X/∂t² is α²∫∇u·∇ü.
- So, up to the factor dt², one minimizes exactly Z.

Minimizing over ü with the constraint div ü = 0 via a multiplier λ gives ü − α²∇²u + ∇λ = 0. That is the vector wave equation for an incompressible elastic ether, with a pressure-like term.
- The bottom of the page carries this out: the term ∫ λ div u dx, varied and integrated by parts, gives −(∂λ/∂x1) δu1.

The line Σ(∂U/∂x1)² + ∫U dm + ∫dm Σ(d²x/dt²)² is the same scheme for masses coupled to a potential field U. It combines field energy ∫|∇U|², interaction ∫U dm, and Gauss constraint of the masses. Varying U gives the Poisson equation (gravitation/electrostatics mediated by a medium).

(B) Vector-analytic preliminaries (middle).
- He takes a field (X1, X2, X3) with Σ ∂X_ι/∂x_ι = 0 and a line integral X1 dx1 + ….
- Stokes' theorem: ∮ X·dx = ∫(∂X1/∂x2 − ∂X2/∂x1) dx1dx2 + ∫(∂X2/∂x3 − …) dx2dx3 + ….
- Δ_1 X = ι1 is solved by a Newtonian potential X = ∫ ι/r dx, with r built from x'_ι − x_ι.
- Green's identity: ∫ λ ∇²λ dx = ∫ Σ(∂λ/∂x_ι)² dx. The correct sign is −, for vanishing boundary terms.

Notation: Δ_1 u := ∂u2/∂x3 − ∂u3/∂x2 (cyclically), i.e. Δ = −curl. The '!' marks this definition, X_1 = Δ_1 u.
He computes Δ_1ΔU and writes it as ∇²u1 − ∂(div u)/∂x1.

(C) Magnetostatics/vector potential by a variational principle (lower half).
The principle is
δ ∫ [ ½ Σ (Δ_ι u)² + u1ι1 + u2ι2 + u3ι3 ] dx = 0,
with compatibility div ι = 0 (noted after the '|').
The variation is Σ Δ_ι u δΔ_ι u = Δ_1u(∂δu2/∂x3 − ∂δu3/∂x2) + Δ_2u(∂δu3/∂x1 − ∂δu1/∂x3) + ….
Integrating by parts, he collects the coefficient of δu1, namely ±(∂Δ_3u/∂x2 − ∂Δ_2u/∂x3). Writing −δu_h Δ_hΔu + ι_h δu_h, he reaches the field equation Δ_1Δu = ι1.
With div u = 0 this becomes ∇²u1 = ι1, solved by
u1 = −(1/4π) ∫ ι1/r dx + ∂μ/∂x1.
The gradient term is gauge freedom. This is the vector potential of a current distribution ι in Coulomb gauge.

A further line reads α ∂u1/∂t + ∂μ/∂x1 + ẋ2(∂u1/∂x2 − ∂u2/∂x1) − ẋ3(…).
- It appears to be the force component on a moving charge: −[−α∂A/∂t − ∇φ + v×curl A]_1, with u as vector potential and μ as scalar potential.
- This is a Lorentz-type force, written with the vector potential.
- The reading of ∂X_2/∂t as a velocity component is my interpretation.

Right column: ∫ c ∂(1/r)/∂p ds and ∫ (∂(1/r)/∂p) dp ∫ (c/r) ds. These are the potential of a double layer (normal derivative p) and of a line current c along s. This is Ampère/Neumann-type material.
errors: Δ_1ΔU: with Δ_1u = ∂u2/∂x3 − ∂u3/∂x2, one has Δ_1(Δu) = ∂(div u)/∂x1 − ∇²u1. Riemann writes the opposite sign, ∇²u1 − ∂1(div u).
In the variation of ½Σ(Δ_ιu)², the coefficient of δu1 after integration by parts is +(∂Δ_2u/∂x3 − ∂Δ_3u/∂x2) = +Δ_1Δu. Riemann writes −δu Δ_1Δu, the opposite sign.
The two sign slips cancel. The true Euler–Lagrange equation is ΔΔu = −ι, i.e. ∇²u = ι for div u = 0, so his final u1 = −(1/4π)∫ι1/r dx + ∂μ/∂x1 is correct.
Green's identity is written ∫λ∇²λ = +∫|∇λ|². With vanishing boundary terms the right side should carry a minus sign; this may be a slip or an omitted sign.
The '½' in front of X is written ambiguously above the line; the factor ½ is needed for the dt²/2 Taylor term to reproduce the α²∇u·∇ü term exactly.
Boundary terms in all integrations by parts are silently dropped. This is standard for unbounded or decaying fields.

results.what: Gauss's principle of least constraint applied to a continuous incompressible elastic medium: minimize ∫½|ü|² + α²∇u·∇ü subject to div ü = 0, giving ü = α²∇²u − ∇λ
results.modern_name: Gauss principle of least constraint for continua / incompressible elastic (ether) wave equation with Lagrange-multiplier pressure
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss 1829 (principle); its use for continua is scattered in 19th-century work

results.what: Field energy + interaction + Gauss constraint for masses coupled to a potential U
results.modern_name: Field-mediated (local) formulation of Newtonian gravitation/electrostatics via a variational principle
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann's own natural-philosophy fragments (Werke, 'Gravitation und Licht'); later field theories

results.what: Stokes' theorem written out in components
results.usually_credited_to: Thomson (Kelvin) 1850, Stokes 1854; Riemann used it in lectures

results.what: curl curl u = grad div u − ∇²u (in Riemann's Δ notation)
results.modern_name: Vector identity curl curl = grad div − Laplacian

results.what: Variational principle δ∫[½|curl u|² + u·ι] = 0 giving curl curl u = −ι, and in Coulomb gauge u = −(1/4π)∫ι/r + ∇μ
results.modern_name: Magnetostatic energy principle for the vector potential (Coulomb gauge), with gauge freedom
results.usually_credited_to: Vector potential: F. Neumann 1845, Kirchhoff 1857, Maxwell 1861–65; variational form: Maxwell/later Lagrangian electrodynamics

results.what: Force on a moving charge as α∂u/∂t + ∇μ + v×curl u terms
results.modern_name: Lorentz force expressed via vector and scalar potentials (E = −∂A/∂t − ∇φ, plus v×B)

results.what: Potentials of double layer and line currents, ∫c ∂(1/r)/∂p ds
results.modern_name: Double-layer potential / Neumann potential of a current loop

deep.surprise_reason: Most of the page is standard potential theory and vector calculus. Riemann's interest in an ether and in variational, field-mediated formulations of gravitation and electrodynamics is documented, in his Gauss-principle fragments and the 1858 retarded-potential paper. Two features are mildly notable. One is the systematic use of Gauss's least-constraint principle for an incompressible continuum, with a multiplier. The other is a vector-potential energy principle (½|curl u|² + u·ι) with Coulomb-gauge solution, plus an apparent v×curl A force term, roughly contemporaneous with Maxwell's 1861–65 work. These are fragmentary, and parts of the reading (the force line) are uncertain, so the surprise is modest.

checkable.sympy: x1,x2,x3=symbols('x1 x2 x3'); u1,u2,u3=[Function(n)(x1,x2,x3) for n in ('u1','u2','u3')]; D=lambda a,b,c:(diff(b,x3)-diff(c,x2), diff(c,x1)-diff(a,x3), diff(a,x2)-diff(b,x1)); X=D(u1,u2,u3); div=diff(u1,x1)+diff(u2,x2)+diff(u3,x3); simplify(D(*X)[0] - (diff(div,x1) - (diff(u1,x1,2)+diff(u1,x2,2)+diff(u1,x3,2))))
checkable.asserts: With Riemann's Δ_1u=∂u2/∂x3−∂u3/∂x2, Δ_1(Δu) = ∂(div u)/∂x1 − ∇²u1 (result 0), showing Riemann's sign is reversed

checkable.sympy: v1,v2,v3=[Function(n)(x1,x2,x3) for n in ('v1','v2','v3')]; Du=D(u1,u2,u3); Dv=D(v1,v2,v3); DDu=D(*Du); C=(diff(u3,x2)-diff(u2,x3), diff(u1,x3)-diff(u3,x1), diff(u2,x1)-diff(u1,x2)); F=(v2*C[2]-v3*C[1], v3*C[0]-v1*C[2], v1*C[1]-v2*C[0]); simplify(sum(a*b for a,b in zip(Du,Dv)) - (v1*DDu[0]+v2*DDu[1]+v3*DDu[2]) - (diff(F[0],x1)+diff(F[1],x2)+diff(F[2],x3)))
checkable.asserts: Δu·Δv − v·ΔΔu is a divergence, so the first variation of ∫½|Δu|² is +∫δu·ΔΔu (result 0)
1/r is harmonic away from 0, underlying u1 = −(1/4π)∫ι1/r dx
Green identity λ∇²λ + |∇λ|² = div(λ∇λ), so ∫λ∇²λ = −∫|∇λ|² for vanishing boundary terms
Integration by parts −u_xx ü = u_x ü_x − (u_x ü)_x, giving the second line of the constraint functional (result 0)

transcription_corrections: Line 2: the squared term is (∂²u/∂t²)², not (∂u/∂t)², and the cross term is (∂²u/∂x_ι²)(∂²u/∂t²), not ·∂u/∂t.
Line 3: the term is (∂u/∂x_ι)(∂³u/∂x_ι∂t²), a third derivative containing ∂t², not ∂²u/∂x_ι∂t.
The isolated '½' belongs to X = ½∫α²Σ(∂u/∂x_ι)² dx (and possibly to the leading ½Σ(ü)²).
'δ∫Σ(d ∂u/∂t)² + X(t+dt) = 0': the leading symbol is a variation sign δ (or d), with d∂u/∂t the change of velocity in time dt.
'Σ∂X_ι/∂x_ι = 0, Δ_ι X = 0': the second may be ΔX = 0 (Laplace) or a curl condition; it is ambiguous in the image.
'Δ_1 X = Δ_1Δu = …' is an equivalence (≡), with Δ_1 X standing for Δ_1 applied to X = Δu.
The coefficient in u1 = −(1/4π)∫ι1/r dx is partly illegible; −1/4π is consistent with the derivation.
In the force line, '∂X_2/∂t' and '∂X_3/∂t' are likely velocities of coordinates (ẋ2, ẋ3), and the last bracket begins (∂u3/∂x1 − …) or (∂u1/∂x3 − …).
'Δ_1Δu = ι_1 | o ∂ι1/∂x1+∂ι2/∂x2+∂ι3/∂x3' should read: Δ_1Δu = ι_1, with condition div ι = 0.
Right-bottom 'Δ_1Δ[−Δ−]u = Δ_1ι' is likely 'Δ_1ΔΔu = Δ_1ι' (curl applied to the field equation), with one Δ possibly struck.
